PullRequest.Title: terminal: Keep extension PATH contributions on their originating host
PullRequest.Body:

Related to #286553. **Draft: live Windows-client/Linux-server acceptance remains pending.**

## Changes

Keep extension PATH contributions on the computer that produced them. The main-thread terminal bridge records its actual extension-host authority, and the existing environment collection service selects matching PATH mutations before merging them for each terminal.

- Preserve same-host contributions, the terminal's base PATH, non-PATH variables, scopes, and mutation options.
- Persist producer identity and exclude unknown/foreign cached PATH from extension-host initialization, preventing later unrelated updates from relabeling old paths.
- Wire fresh local/remote launches, local revival environment/options, and terminal relaunch comparisons through the same target-aware collection.
- Preserve the existing remote historical-process recovery behavior until normal relaunch.
- Document the uniform PATH-locality and cache-migration compatibility changes.

The current native Rust shim still contributes its directory through the extension's terminal service. No Rust implementation, launcher scripts, public API signatures, RPC formats, settings, or policies change here.

## Compatibility and recovery

This intentionally changes PATH sharing for **all** extensions: a contribution no longer applies to terminals on another computer. Other environment variables retain their existing sharing behavior.

Old cached extension PATH entries have no trusted producer identity and are withheld until refreshed, including from the extension's initial cached API view. A terminal opened before the refresh may require normal relaunch. Independently installed commands and base PATH are not removed.

Recovered remote process snapshots retain their historical complete environment; an affected pre-fix recovered terminal needs normal relaunch to pick up the fix. There is no forced restart.

Before production edits, the bridge/process regressions failed on foreign/legacy PATH replay and application. Test setup/type failures encountered during authoring were fixed separately; they were not counted as bug evidence.

Independent code review found a stale terminal-status case after attachment fallback/strict launch. Parent-run regressions reproduced both status failures before the repair; the full suite, type-check, and lint passed again afterward.

The first client build found an installed SDK/runtime mismatch; `npm run install-fast` passed and restored the expected dependencies without tracked dependency changes. Subsequent builds passed.

## Pending live acceptance

Not run in this macOS session:

- [ ] Windows client connected to Linux using a build containing the native shim.
- [ ] Both extension execution locations and both remote/local terminal targets.
- [ ] `type -a code` and `code <temporary-file>` opening the client editor.
- [ ] A sentinel executable in the last base PATH entry before terminal creation.
- [ ] Legacy cached contributions, historical remote recovery, and normal relaunch.

The current Rust integration appends, whereas the old implementation prepended. The source-level reproduction establishes corruption and command-lookup failures, but does not establish the original reporter's exact extension-host/cache provenance or reproduce the old first-entry symptom unchanged in a live current build.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: MainThreadTerminalService builds the target-authority snapshot and serializes it before the extension host receives its initial cached collection. Later extension mutations cross the extension-host RPC immediately, while terminal notifications are debounced for one second and persistence is throttled.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Initialize the extension host with serialized environment-variable collections
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One initialization call per extension host, carrying one grouped snapshot rather than one call per extension or mutator.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same single initialization IPC serialized all collections without authority filtering; the diff filters before serialization and can reduce payload size.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The extension host's initial cached environment collection waits for this serialization and IPC, as before.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Synchronize an extension's collection mutation to the main thread
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One RPC per effective collection mutation; unchanged by this diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Identical RPC frequency and full-collection serialization.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The main-thread service updates its in-memory collection before subsequent terminal creation can use it.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist grouped extension environment collections through workspace storage
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Throttled to at most one persistence operation per second across collection changes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same throttled write occurred; the serialized record now includes a small authority field.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Not on terminal notification critical path beyond the existing synchronous storage-service call behavior.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of installed extensions with terminal environment collections and total mutators/descriptions; effective authority cardinality is normally local plus the window's remote authority.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Initial bridge construction is synchronous per extension host. Collection mutations may arrive in bursts, but terminal notifications are debounced and each authority rebuild is coalesced through the shared map.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold authority views perform O(extensions + mutators) filtering/merge work; warm consumers are O(1) cache lookups. Any real collection update invalidates the views, while the one-second notification debounce prevents rebuild fanout for mutation bursts.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed lines, cache invalidation, debounce, and RPC call sites were traced directly.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact extension and mutator counts vary, but repository code explicitly expects collections to be small; no new per-item boundary or unbounded authority source was found.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The diff adds bounded CPU/allocation for a cold authority view, reuses it across consumers, and does not increase IPC or persistence cardinality.

Scenarios.Scenario: Fresh local or remote terminal launch and relaunch
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Resolve the profile/base environment, apply the cached authority-specific merged collection, serialize launch options, then cross the local or remote terminal-process boundary to create one process.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create a local pty process with one serialized options object
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One backend createProcess call per terminal; all eligible collections are grouped into that request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same single create call and collection serialization occurred; the diff changes only which PATH entries are included and suppresses collections for strict environments.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Process startup waits for the existing pty-host IPC/subprocess creation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create a remote terminal through RemoteTerminalChannelClient
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One channel call per remote terminal, with all collections grouped into one payload.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same grouped request serialized all service collections; the diff substitutes the cached target-authority view and can omit work for strict-environment launches.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Remote terminal startup waits for configuration resolution, authority resolution, and this existing grouped create request.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Spawn the terminal shell via the pty host
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One shell process per terminal launch.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: One shell process was spawned with the unfiltered merged environment.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: This is the terminal availability critical path, unchanged in count or scheduling.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One launch request, total eligible environment mutators, and workspace-scoped entries; effective boundary cardinality remains one process creation per terminal.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each terminal launch follows its own async chain. The diff adds no shared burst or new per-mutator asynchronous work; remote creation remains one grouped channel request.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold launch after a mutation pays one O(total mutators) authority-view build; warm launches share it. There is no negative-cache retry because filtered empty collections are cached as valid merged views.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: both local and remote launch call paths and serialization helpers were inspected.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Terminal and mutator counts vary, but the changed work is grouped and cached; no realistic multiplicative boundary increase was found.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Process/IPC cardinality is unchanged, filtered payloads are no larger, and authority merge work is coalesced.

Scenarios.Scenario: Persistent terminal attachment, failed attachment fallback, and normal relaunch
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Attempt one backend attachment first. A successful attachment now skips environment resolution; only a failed attachment resolves the fresh target environment and proceeds to normal process creation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Attach to an existing local or remote persistent process
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One attach request per restored terminal.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same attach call was made, but environment resolution ran before it even when the result was unused.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: A successful attachment can make progress without the former preliminary environment-resolution await.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create a replacement terminal process after attachment failure
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one create request for each failed attach.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Fallback also resolved and created a process; the diff moves resolution later so successful attachments avoid it.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Fallback waits for fresh environment resolution and then process creation, preserving necessary ordering.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One operation per restored terminal; environment work scales with eligible mutators only on fallback/relaunch.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Attachment is serialized before fallback creation for each terminal. The diff does not launch attachment and creation concurrently and therefore introduces no resource burst.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Successful attachment does not need a new target view unless status comparison requires it; fallback/relaunch shares the service cache.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the before/after ordering is explicit in the changed hunk.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Attachment frequency and backend latency vary, but the only scheduling change removes work from the successful path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No regression; this path is performance-neutral on fallback and faster on successful attachment.

Scenarios.Scenario: Local persistent-terminal revival during window startup
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Read one persisted state blob, resolve fresh environments for all revived terminals, serialize current target collections into each eligible state, then send one grouped reviveTerminalProcesses IPC before layout restoration completes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read and parse the persisted terminal buffer-state blob from workspace storage
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One grouped read for all persisted terminals.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same grouped state was read and parsed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Startup revival requires this existing read before environments can be refreshed.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Revive all persisted terminal processes in the pty host
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One IPC containing N terminal states, not one IPC per state.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same grouped IPC already carried each state's persisted environmentVariableCollections options; the diff refreshes those arrays before sending rather than adding a new field or call.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Terminal restoration waits for this grouped IPC, as before.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restore persisted terminal layout after revival when present
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one grouped layout call.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs after process revival and is unchanged by the collection filtering logic.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of persisted local terminals N and eligible environment mutators M. The added in-memory serialization is O(N*M), while the grouped IPC and process revival cardinality remain unchanged.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Per-terminal environment resolution remains under the pre-existing Promise.all, so effective concurrency is N. The diff adds synchronous serialization within each existing task but no new asynchronous boundary or limiter bypass.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The merged target view is shared across all N states, but serialization creates fresh arrays per eligible state. This is bounded by the already persisted per-state collection payload and does not create retained cache growth.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the O(N*M) in-memory serialization and unchanged boundary counts; low uncertainty only concerns its negligible expected magnitude.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Large N and M could add startup CPU/allocation, but realistic collections are small and the pre-diff state already carried one serialized collection per terminal; evidence does not establish user-visible latency or memory growth.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. The added per-state serialization is a bounded refresh of an already per-state payload, with no new I/O/IPC fanout or retention mechanism.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: Read the persisted remote state and send it unchanged in one grouped revive request; authority filtering takes effect only on a later normal relaunch.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read persisted remote terminal buffer state
Revive all historical remote terminal processes
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One grouped remote channel call for all states.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same historical payload and call; the PR intentionally does not re-resolve remote environments here.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Remote restoration waits for this call, unchanged.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of persisted remote terminal states in the single serialized blob.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One grouped remote revival request; no per-terminal requests are introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No filtering cache lookup occurs until a normal relaunch or fresh terminal creation.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the remote revival implementation was inspected and contains no changed filtering work.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Remote state size varies, but the diff does not change payload construction or request count on this path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance regression; remote historical recovery retains its existing grouped I/O and IPC behavior.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass across all 15 changed files. Traced authority-view construction/invalidation, extension-host synchronization, active-terminal update fanout, fresh local/remote launch, persistent attach fallback, and local/remote revival. No high-confidence actionable performance regression was introduced, and no finding was submitted.
